passages.t: Cyrus the anointed, and light and darkness
passages.happening:
‘This is what the LORD says to Cyrus His anointed, whose right hand I have grasped to subdue nations before him’ (verse 1), to disarm kings and open doors so that the gates will not be shut. ‘I will go before you and level the mountains; I will break down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron’ (verse 2). God will give him hidden treasures, ‘so that you may know that I am the LORD, the God of Israel, who calls you by name’ (verse 3).

For the sake of Jacob his servant, God calls Cyrus by name and gives him a title of honor, ‘though you have not known Me’ (verse 4). ‘I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me’ (verse 5). He will equip Cyrus, so that from sunrise to sunset all may know there is no other (verses 5-6).

‘I form the light and create the darkness; I bring prosperity and create calamity. I, the LORD, do all these things’ (verse 7). Let the heavens rain righteousness and the earth sprout salvation (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Anointed, mashiach, is the word behind Messiah, and in the Old Testament it is used of kings, priests and others set apart for God's purpose. Here it is given to a foreign king who does not know the LORD. Cyrus is anointed for one task: to set God's people free.

Cyrus's capture of Babylon in 539 BC was swift, and the city fell almost without a fight. Gates of bronze and bars of iron, the defenses of great cities, are no obstacle to the one God sends.

The repeated line, there is no other, is the drumbeat of these chapters. Even Cyrus's victories are meant to show the whole world that the LORD alone is God.
passages.later: Ezra records that ‘the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia’ (Ezra 1:1) to send out his decree. And Jeremiah hears God call Nebuchadnezzar ‘My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon’ (Jeremiah 27:6), as Isaiah calls Cyrus God's anointed.
passages.hard:
Does verse 7 mean that God creates evil?

Older English translations, such as the King James Version, have God say that he creates evil, which has troubled many readers. Most interpreters agree that the Hebrew word ra here means calamity or disaster, set against shalom, well-being, in the same line, not moral wickedness. In its setting, God is claiming that the rise and fall of nations, including the disaster coming on Babylon and the prosperity coming to Israel, are in his hands. Some interpreters suggest the verse also answers a view of the world in which good and evil are rival powers. Isaiah allows no second power.

This does not settle every question about God and evil. Scripture elsewhere insists that God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13) while holding that nothing happens outside his rule. Christians have held these together in different ways, some stressing God's ordaining of all things and others his permission of what he does not cause. The verse is about God's rule over history, and it is meant as comfort: no dark power can overturn God's purpose. It is not a key for saying that any particular calamity is God's verdict on those who suffer it.
passages.asks: God called Cyrus by name and used him, though Cyrus did not know him. Ask where God may be at work through people you would not expect. And ask what it means for you that there is no dark power that can overturn God's purpose.

passages.t: The clay and the potter, and a God who hides himself
passages.happening:
‘Woe to him who quarrels with his Maker’ (verse 9), one clay pot among many. Does the clay ask the potter what he is making? Woe to anyone who asks a father or mother what they have brought into the world (verse 10).

The Holy One of Israel asks, ‘How dare you question Me about My sons, or instruct Me in the work of My hands?’ (verse 11). He made the earth and stretched out the heavens (verse 12). ‘I will raise up Cyrus in righteousness, and I will make all his ways straight. He will rebuild My city and set My exiles free, but not for payment or reward’ (verse 13).

The wealth of Egypt, Cush and the Sabeans will come to Israel, and they will confess that God is with them and there is no other (verse 14). ‘Truly You are a God who hides Himself, O God of Israel, the Savior’ (verse 15). The makers of idols will go off in disgrace (verse 16), ‘But Israel will be saved by the LORD with an everlasting salvation’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The prophet expects that some in Israel will object to God's plan of using a pagan king, and he answers them. The answer is the old picture of the potter and the clay. The pot does not tell the potter how to shape it.

Cyrus will free the exiles without being paid for it.

Verse 15 is a striking confession. God hides himself: his ways are not obvious, and he works through unexpected people like Cyrus. Yet he is the Savior. The first hearers had felt God hidden through the long exile. The prophet does not deny it. He says the hidden God is still the one who saves.
passages.later: Paul uses the same picture: ‘Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it’ that he made it wrongly (Romans 9:20)? And a psalm prays, ‘Why, O LORD, do You stand far off? Why do You hide in times of trouble?’ (Psalm 10:1).
passages.asks: The prophet calls God a God who hides himself and the Savior in the same breath. Ask whether God feels hidden to you now. And ask whether you can trust that the hidden God is still saving.

passages.t: An invitation to all the ends of the earth
passages.happening:
The LORD who created the heavens and formed the earth did not make it to be empty, but formed it to be lived in. ‘I am the LORD, and there is no other’ (verse 18). He has not spoken in secret or told Jacob to seek him in vain; he speaks the truth (verse 19).

‘Come, gather together, and draw near, you fugitives from the nations’ (verse 20). Those who carry wooden idols pray to a god that cannot save. Who foretold this long ago? Was it not the LORD? There is no God but him, a righteous God and Savior (verse 21).

‘Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other’ (verse 22). God has sworn by himself, a word that will not be taken back: ‘Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance’ (verse 23). They will say that in the LORD alone are righteousness and strength (verse 24). ‘In the LORD all descendants of Israel will be justified and will exult’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The chapter widens from Cyrus and Israel to the whole world. The fugitives from the nations, people uprooted by the empires as Israel was, are invited too.

Verse 22 is one of the widest invitations in the Old Testament, to all the ends of the earth. The God who alone is God is not a tribal god. He is the Savior of all who turn to him.

The oath of verse 23 pictures every knee bowing and every tongue swearing allegiance. The first hearers, a small and scattered people, were told that their God would one day be confessed by the whole world.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 23 twice: ‘every knee will bow before Me; every tongue will confess to God’ (Romans 14:11), and of Jesus, ‘that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow’ (Philippians 2:10).
passages.asks: God invites all the ends of the earth to turn to him and be saved. Ask whether you think of God's invitation as wide enough to include the people you find hardest to imagine there. And ask whether you have turned to him yourself.
